title: JavaScript formatting: quotes, semicolons and minification
description: Site JS formatter (Prettier) and minifier (Terser): semicolons, quotes, number normalization, trailing commas, parser limits, and why neither replaces tests.
content:
The site's JavaScript formatter re-prints code with Prettier, while the Minify button uses Terser: one adds semicolons, swaps quotes and adds indentation; the other renames, folds constants and removes dead code. This article covers which characters each operation touches, which syntax the parser accepts, and what neither can guarantee.

One page, two engines

Two buttons sit on top of two libraries. Formatting dynamically imports the standalone build of Prettier and then loads the babel and estree plugins; Minify dynamically imports Terser and calls minify(). Both load only when you click; on the first format the status bar reads "Loading formatter engine (about 1MB on first run)..." (that is the page's wording, not a measured value) — this run recorded three scripts totaling 610677 bytes, about 0.6 MB.

Formatting options are hard-coded: parser is babel, semi and singleQuote are true, tabWidth is 2, printWidth is 100; the page has no dropdown or checkbox to change them. Minify passes only mangle: true and compress: true, not toplevel, so Terser's default toplevel: false is left untouched.

When the input is empty, both buttons only show "Please enter JavaScript code." and do not clear the previous output; the output is cleared only when parsing or minification fails, and the status bar then reads "Parsing failed:" or "Minification failed:".

Formatting changes more than whitespace

Feed the 102-character minified snippet from the sample into the formatter and the output becomes 115 characters: semicolons go from 2 to 3, double quotes from 8 to 0, single quotes from 0 to 8. The extra characters come mostly from spaces around operators, line breaks and indentation, but those are not the only characters that change.

Semicolons: a statement that ends without a semicolon gets one, but a function declaration gets no semicolon after its own closing brace. Quotes: singleQuote: true makes double-quoted strings use single quotes, but the rule prefers whichever form needs fewer escapes; const a = "it's"; contains a single quote inside, so switching to single quotes would need escaping, and the double quotes stay. Quotes on JSX attributes are unaffected by this setting and remain double quotes.

Object keys are handled as-needed: {"a":1,"a-b":2,"1":3} becomes { a: 1, 'a-b': 2, 1: 3 }. Number literals are normalized too: 0XFF becomes 0xff, .5 becomes 0.5, 1. becomes 1, while 1e3, 0b101, 0o17 and 1_000 keep their original form. Parameterless new expressions get parentheses, so new Date becomes new Date().

Consecutive blank lines collapse into one, and a single newline is added at the end of the file. Comments are kept: line comments stay where they were, block comments move with the code next to them. Spaces and newlines inside template literals, and the characters inside ordinary strings, are not changed.

Long parameter lists over printWidth: 100 are wrapped, with a trailing comma on the last item; in this run a long call was split into 7 lines (the first line, 5 parameter lines and the closing line), the longest only 34 characters. The trailing comma is not an extra switch on this page but the result of Prettier 3's default trailingComma: "all" — single-line structures do not get one.

Format the formatted output a second time and it comes out identical; code minified onto one line also expands normally. Formatting can be run repeatedly, but it re-lays out the whole file every time, not just the selected part.

Parser limits: what babel accepts, and what it does not

The parser is babel, with only the babel and estree plugins and no TypeScript plugin. So const a: number = 1; fails outright: the status bar shows "Parsing failed: Unexpected token (1:8)" and the output box is emptied. This is not a logic error in the code, it is the parser not recognizing type annotations; the page offers no way to switch to the typescript parser.

More syntax is accepted than you might expect: JSX passes, and its attributes still use double quotes; class private fields pass; class decorators pass, with a class decorator placed on its own line; top-level await passes; optional chaining and nullish coalescing pass. Prettier's documentation states that support for non-standard syntax is best-effort and may change between releases, so the boundary is whatever the page actually returns.

  • JSX: passes, and the output keeps structures like <div className="a">hi</div>.
  • Class private fields: #x = 1; and this.#x are preserved verbatim.
  • Class decorators: @sealed and class A {} are printed on two separate lines.
  • Top-level await: await fetch('/x'); passes.
  • TypeScript type annotations: fail, the output is cleared and an error position is given.

Minification changes names and structure

Minify goes through Terser, with mangle and compress on by default. The 139-character function addNumbers(firstNumber, secondNumber) becomes 85 characters after minification, 38.8% less: the two parameters are renamed to e and r and the body is squeezed onto one line; the top-level function name addNumbers and the top-level constant result are preserved, because toplevel is not enabled.

compress folds constants: const a = 1 + 2; becomes const a=3, and "a" + "b" becomes "ab"; dead code such as if (false) inside a function is removed, and return x * 2 becomes return 2*n. An unused top-level let unused = 5 is not removed by default — dropping unused top-level variables also needs toplevel: true.

Renaming changes information that is observable at runtime: the inner named function innerHelper becomes anonymous after minification, and reading .name after eval returns an empty string; the function body's toString also shrinks from 54 characters to 42. Code that depends on Function.prototype.name or on source text (some dependency-injection and test frameworks, for example) is affected; Terser's keep_fnames exists for exactly this case, but the page does not expose it.

Scopes that contain eval are treated specially: when a function calls eval(userInput), neither userInput nor localSecret is renamed, because renaming could break eval's lookup of variables by name. Ordinary comments are removed and license comments starting with /*! are kept; numbers and quotes are minified too, so 1000 becomes 1e3, 0.5 becomes .5, and strings containing double quotes are rewritten with single quotes. Minified output has no trailing newline.

Formatting is not minification: opposite goals

Both buttons change source text, in opposite directions. Formatting serves readability and code review, so its output is usually longer; minification serves transfer size, so its output is shorter, and it renames and deletes code. In this sample, formatting the code and then minifying it produced output byte-for-byte identical to minifying the original directly: whether you format before minifying does not change the minified result; the other way round, formatting a minified result only yields a readable version, and cannot bring back the original source.

DimensionFormatter (Prettier)Minifier (Terser)
Primary goalReadable, consistent styleFewer bytes
Whitespace and indentationRe-laid out as indented linesRedundant whitespace removed
Semicolons and quotesSemicolons added, quotes unifiedOmittable whitespace and semicolons removed, shorter quote style used
NamesUntouchedLocal variables, parameters and inner function names renamed
CommentsKeptOrdinary comments removed, /*! kept
Trailing newlineYesNo
Observable informationSource text and toString text change, behavior does notSource text, Function.name, toString and comments change, behavior and results do not

The last row of the table is the key when choosing: formatting treats "behavior unchanged" as a correctness requirement; minification aims to keep runtime results the same, but does not promise that names, source text and comments stay intact.

Limits and boundaries

Start with what the messages mean. "Formatting complete" only says babel parsed the code and Prettier printed it; it does not mean there is no logic error and no type error, nor that the code matches the team's lint rules; "Minification complete" likewise only says Terser could parse and minify the code.

Parser limit: only JavaScript syntax that babel supports can be parsed. Type annotations from TypeScript and from Flow both fail, and syntax babel does not know fails at the parse stage with an error position (in this run both kinds of annotation were tried, and for Flow a variable annotation was added as well; the status bar read "Parsing failed" every time); the page has no option to switch parsers. Non-standard syntax such as decorators currently passes, but that support is best-effort and may change with an upgrade.

Not configurable: semi, singleQuote, tabWidth and printWidth are fixed, trailingComma takes Prettier's default, so an existing team style cannot be applied; the minifier's toplevel, keep_fnames and source map options are not exposed either. To match a repository's configuration, run it locally with the project's own Prettier and Terser configuration rather than treating the page output as the final style.

Formatting is not minification, and it does not replace tests. Formatted output is usually longer (in this run 102 characters became 115), and minification renames symbols and changes Function.name and toString text; before shipping formatted or minified code, tests and a build still have to run.

Local processing: the tool page only reads and writes the text boxes in the browser. During the 47 cases in this run there were 17 requests in total, all GETs to 127.0.0.1, with no request bodies and no request that uploaded code; input is not kept after a refresh or when the page is closed.

Judging the result before taking it back to a project

If the goal is code that reads well and diffs that stay stable, use formatting: it keeps comments and only re-lays out whitespace and a few characters, which suits a style pass before committing; but its trailing comma and quote rules may differ from the repository's configuration, so after copying back, let the project's own Prettier run once more.

If the goal is a smaller payload, use minification — but measure the gain first: in this run the sample went from 139 characters to 85, 38.8% less, and in a real project you also have to count the difference after gzip. Minified output suits build artifacts, not repository source; when function names must survive, use the project's Terser configuration with keep_fnames or turn mangle off.

Several neighboring tools on the site can be used alongside: for stylesheets use the CSS formatter, to inspect JSON structure use the JSON formatter, to tidy an HTML fragment use the HTML formatter; when you need to verify a replacement rule rather than re-lay out code, use the regex tester. Each has its own parser and whitespace handling, so do not assume the same input gives the same result across them.

Whether a result is usable is judged by comparison, not by the status bar: run the same expressions before and after formatting, call the same arguments before and after minification, and confirm the behavior and results stay the same; also check Function.name, toString and comments, which do change as described above. This run covered only a limited set of samples.

faqs.q: Why does formatting add trailing commas?
faqs.a: Prettier 3 defaults trailingComma to "all", and the tool does not change that setting, so the last item of a multi-line object, array or parameter list gets a comma, while single-line structures do not. If the team style forbids trailing commas, run the output through the project's own Prettier configuration; the page has no switch to turn this off.

faqs.q: Why does TypeScript code fail to parse?
faqs.a: The parser is fixed to babel and only the babel and estree plugins are loaded, with no TypeScript plugin, so type annotations fail at the parse stage: the status bar gives a position such as Unexpected token and the output is cleared. The tool does no type checking; convert the code to JavaScript or remove the annotations to format it.

faqs.q: Why do function names change after minification, and can they be restored?
faqs.a: Terser enables mangle by default, so local variables, parameters and inner function names are shortened or made anonymous, which changes Function.name and the text from toString; top-level names are preserved by default because the page does not enable toplevel. Minification is one-way: the page keeps no mapping and has no source map or keep_fnames option.

faqs.q: Does "Formatting complete" mean the code is fine?
faqs.a: No. It only means babel parsed the code and Prettier printed it; no type checking, lint run or logic validation happens. Syntactically valid code can still have runtime errors, and TypeScript annotations fail to parse at all. Run tests, type checks and a build before publishing.

focus: Formatting adds semicolons, swaps quotes, and normalizes numbers and trailing commas; minification renames and folds constants. Both change source text and toString text, and only minification changes Function.name; formatting keeps behavior unchanged, while the babel parser does not accept TypeScript or Flow type annotations.
notice: Formatting and minification both run locally in the browser; every request recorded in this run was a GET for local static assets and no request uploaded code; the "Formatting complete" message only means parsing and printing succeeded, not that the code is correct.
